summary:
The "Think Differently About Emergencies Act" (Pub. L. 118-123, H.R. 6249, enacted November 25, 2024) is a reporting-and-review statute directing the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the Comptroller General to assess FEMA's disaster-related assistance to individuals with disabilities. The Act creates no new grant authority, appropriates no funds, and amends no existing U.S. Code provision; it operates solely through mandated reporting and review obligations.

Section 1 sets the short title.

Section 2 imposes a one-time reporting requirement. Not later than 120 days after enactment, the FEMA Administrator must submit to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs a report describing assistance and resources FEMA provides—to States, localities, nonprofit organizations, and directly to affected individuals—for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families impacted by major disasters declared under section 401 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5170). Subsection (b) enumerates required contents: (1) available resources and best practices; (2) the process for training and deploying personnel to coordinate with States, localities, and nonprofits; (3) a count of FEMA programs supporting such individuals in preparing for and recovering from disasters, including accommodations; (4) a description of FEMA outreach to State, local, and nonprofit experts; and (5) identification of areas for improvement.

Section 3 establishes a separate review obligation with a longer deadline. Not later than one year after enactment, the Comptroller General and the FEMA Administrator must each independently (1) conduct a review of assistance and resources FEMA provides to States, localities, nonprofits, and individuals to assist individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities, individuals with physical disabilities, and the families of both; (2) identify potential legal impediments to providing such assistance; (3) provide Congress recommendations on improving assistance, enhancing coordination with States, localities, and nonprofits, and streamlining the application process and delivery; and (4) provide recommendations on any necessary legislative reform. Notably, Section 3 expands the covered population beyond Section 2 by including individuals with physical disabilities.

The Act contains no authorization of appropriations, no sunset provision, and no substantive amendment to the Stafford Act or other statutes; its sole enforceable elements are the 120-day and one-year deadlines governing the respective report and reviews.
